mainLabels.label: Enemy Image
mainLabels.description: Enemy Image describes how language can portray an outgroup as an enemy. The group appears dangerous, immoral, or fundamentally different. This can make violence against them seem more acceptable, reduce moral hesitation, and mobilize the ingroup.

subLabels.label: Homogenization
subLabels.description: Homogenization describes how language can make an outgroup appear as one single, uniform group. Individual differences become less visible. As a result, the actions, traits, or perceived threat of some individuals may be projected onto the whole group. This can blur the distinction between civilians and combatants.

subLabels.label: Immutability
subLabels.description: Immutability describes linguistic patterns that present an outgroup as unchangeable in its nature, ideology, or threat. The group appears as if it cannot reform, coexist peacefully, or be reached through compromise. If an outgroup is portrayed as permanently dangerous or hostile, peaceful solutions can seem naive, impossible, or even risky. This can make harder measures appear more necessary or justified.

subLabels.label: Essentialization
subLabels.description: Essentialization means that an outgroup is presented as having a negative nature. It is not only about individual actions, but about how the whole group is described. The group is linked to certain traits, behaviors, or values. This makes it appear fundamentally different from the ingroup. Essentialization can also be indirect. For example, cruel or abusive treatment of children can create a very negative image of the whole group, because children stand for innocence and vulnerability. Such portrayals can make violence against the outgroup seem more acceptable or necessary.

subLabels.label: Dehumanization
subLabels.description: Dehumanization describes language that presents an outgroup as less than fully human. This can happen when people are compared to animals, pests, diseases, objects, or described as inferior. For example, they may be called “vermin” or described as a “disease.” Their suffering may then seem less important or less real. Violence against them can appear less disturbing, more acceptable, or easier to justify. In this way, dehumanization can help mobilize the ingroup by reducing moral hesitation.

subLabels.label: Threat Depiction
subLabels.description: Threat Depiction describes how language can present an outgroup as a threat to the ingroup, its safety, values, territory, or future. The threat is often linked to a demanded action or measure. This can make certain responses appear necessary, protective, or justified. Once an outgroup is framed as dangerous, people may interpret later information through this threat image. Details that confirm the threat can seem more believable, while contradicting information may receive less attention.

mainLabels.label: Just Cause
mainLabels.description: Just Cause describes linguistic patterns that frame violent or harmful measures as rational, necessary, or morally justified. By linking a measure to a specific cause, these statements create a logic of justification in which violence can appear legitimate rather than arbitrary.

subLabels.label: Security rationale
subLabels.description: Security Rationale describes how language can present violent, harmful, or controlling measures as necessary for the security and protection of the ingroup. The focus is not mainly on depicting a threat, but on using security as a reason for action. In this way, such measures can appear reasonable, defensive, or legitimate.

subLabels.label: Self-defence / counterterrorism
subLabels.description: Self-Defence / Counter-Terrorism describes how language can justify violent or harmful measures by framing them as self-defence or counter-terrorism. The focus is not on depicting a threat alone, but on how this threat is used to justify a concrete action. As a result, the measure can appear legitimate, necessary or even defensive.

subLabels.label: Retaliation
subLabels.description: Retaliation describes how language can make harmful measures appear justified as a response to harm attributed to the outgroup. The central logic is: because “they” have harmed us, our response seems deserved, understandable, or necessary. Unlike Self-Defence / Counter-Terrorism, the focus is not mainly on protection from a threat or fighting terrorism. Instead, the measure is framed as a reaction, punishment, or pressure in response to what the outgroup has done.

mainLabels.label: Individual Needs
mainLabels.description: Individual Needs describes rhetorical patterns that appeal to personal needs within the ingroup. These patterns can encourage support, participation, or sacrifice by making people feel needed, respected, hopeful, or part of a meaningful collective mission.

subLabels.label: Meaning
subLabels.description: Meaning is coded for statements in which actions, measures, or willingness to sacrifice are presented as part of a larger meaning-making cause. This can include historical narratives, religious goals or prophecies, or morally significant acts such as saving the nation, religion, or civilization.

subLabels.label: Status
subLabels.description: Status describes statements that emphasize strength, rank, recognition, or national self-assertion.

subLabels.label: Hope for victory
subLabels.description: Hope for Victory describes how language can make victory or success seem possible and close. This can give the ingroup hope, help people keep going, and prevent defeatism.

mainLabels.label: Rhetorical Foreclosure
mainLabels.description: Rhetorical Foreclosure describes linguistic patterns that exclude or devalue alternatives, criticism, or moral concerns. This narrows the space for doubt, reflection, and opposition. In conflict situations, this strategy can be especially effective because people may question messages less critically and place more trust in authorities.

subLabels.label: No alternative framing
subLabels.description: No Alternative Framing describes how language can make a measure appear unavoidable. By suggesting that there is “no choice” or “no other way,” the statement closes down alternatives and makes the action seem necessary rather than debatable.

subLabels.label: Humanity as weakness
subLabels.description: Humanity as Weakness describes statements that present humanity, mercy, empathy, or restraint as weak, insufficient, or irresponsible. This pattern devalues compassion and makes harshness appear more appropriate or necessary than humanity.

subLabels.label: External criticism rejection
subLabels.description: External Criticism Rejection describes statements that dismiss outside criticism as illegitimate, hostile, or antisemitic. This can make external pressure or moral objections appear invalid and protect the ingroup from outside influence.
